topics.title: Resumption Test / Revision of Last Session Work resumption test questions.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall previous term's concepts in catering craft practice, identify different cooking methods and techniques, explain safety procedures in the kitchen, and solve practical problems related to food preparation.

Introduction:
As we begin this new term, it is important to refresh our knowledge on the fundamental concepts we covered last term. This revision will help us build a stronger foundation for the more advanced topics we will be studying this term.

Content:
The resumption test will cover key areas from last term's curriculum, including kitchen safety and hygiene, cooking methods, food preservation techniques, menu planning basics, and equipment usage. Students should review topics such as the different types of cuts for vegetables, the principles of baking, and the importance of proper food storage. The test will include both theoretical questions and practical components where students may be asked to demonstrate specific cooking techniques or identify kitchen equipment. Students should also be prepared to answer questions about nutritional values of different food groups and how they affect meal planning.

Class activity:
Students will be divided into small groups and given a scenario where they need to plan a simple menu for a family of four using local ingredients available in a typical Nigerian market. Each group will present their menu and explain the nutritional considerations behind their choices.

Evaluation questions:
1. List three essential kitchen safety rules that every caterer must follow.
2. Explain the difference between boiling and steaming as cooking methods.
3. Why is proper food storage important in catering practice?
4. Describe how you would prepare yam for frying in a commercial kitchen.
5. A client requests a meal that is both nutritious and affordable for a family of six with limited income. What factors would you consider when planning this meal?

Summary:
Today's revision session has helped us refresh our understanding of fundamental catering concepts that will be essential throughout this term.

topics.title: Meal Planning
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define meal planning, list the importance of meal planning, identify and explain factors affecting meal planning, and apply these factors to create a balanced meal plan for a typical Nigerian family.

Introduction:
Building on our previous knowledge of nutrition and food preparation, we now move to the systematic process of meal planning. This skill is essential for both home economics and professional catering.

Content:
Meal planning is the process of organizing meals in advance to ensure nutritional balance, proper budgeting, and efficient use of resources. The importance of meal planning includes: ensuring nutritional adequacy for all family members, reducing food waste through proper purchasing and storage, saving time and energy in meal preparation, helping to manage household budget effectively, and promoting variety in diet to prevent monotony. Several factors affect meal planning: family size and composition (children, adults, elderly), available budget (considering current market prices of food items), cultural and religious practices (halal, kosher, vegetarian preferences), seasonality of ingredients (mango season, tomato season), cooking facilities available (gas stove, electric cooker, traditional hearth), and time available for preparation. For example, a meal plan for a Nigerian family might include: breakfast - akara with pap and bread, lunch - jollof rice with chicken and fried plantain, dinner - eba with ogbono soup and fish. This plan considers nutritional balance, cost-effectiveness, and cultural preferences.

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to create a one-week meal plan for a family of four with a budget of ₦15,000. They must consider breakfast, lunch, and dinner for seven days, ensuring nutritional balance while staying within budget. They should also list the quantities of each ingredient needed.

Evaluation questions:
1. Define meal planning and explain its importance in catering.
2. List and explain four factors that affect meal planning in a Nigerian household.
3. How would you modify a meal plan for a family with a member who has diabetes?
4. Create a balanced dinner menu for a family of six using ingredients commonly found in a Nigerian market.
5. Explain how meal planning helps in reducing food waste in a catering establishment.

Summary:
Meal planning is a systematic process that considers multiple factors to create nutritious, balanced, and cost-effective meals for individuals and families.

topics.title: Special Menu - Vegetarians
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify different types of vegetarians, explain reasons for vegetarianism, and plan appropriate meals for vegetarians considering their nutritional needs.

Introduction:
As we explore special dietary needs in catering, vegetarianism represents an important consideration. Many Nigerians are adopting vegetarian diets for various reasons, making this knowledge essential for modern caterers.

Content:
Vegetarianism is the practice of abstaining from the consumption of meat, poultry, and sometimes other animal products. There are several types of vegetarians: Lacto-ovo vegetarians consume dairy products and eggs but avoid meat, poultry, and fish; Lacto vegetarians consume dairy products but avoid eggs, meat, poultry, and fish; Ovo vegetarians consume eggs but avoid dairy products, meat, poultry, and fish; Vegans avoid all animal products including dairy, eggs, honey, and gelatin; and Pesco vegetarians consume fish and other seafood but avoid meat and poultry. People adopt vegetarianism for various reasons: health concerns (reducing risk of heart disease, hypertension, and certain cancers), religious beliefs (some traditional African religions prohibit certain meats), environmental concerns (reducing carbon footprint), and ethical reasons (opposition to animal cruelty). When planning meals for vegetarians, caterers must ensure adequate protein intake using beans, lentils, tofu, and nuts; include iron-rich foods like spinach and fortified cereals; provide calcium sources such as leafy greens, fortified plant milks, and sesame seeds; and ensure adequate vitamin B12 through fortified foods or supplements. A typical Nigerian vegetarian menu might include: breakfast - beans porridge with plantain and avocado, lunch - fried rice with mixed vegetables and egg, dinner - efo riro with mushrooms and smoked fish.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to create a three-course vegetarian menu suitable for a Nigerian wedding reception. The menu must include appetizers, main courses, and desserts that are both culturally appropriate and nutritionally balanced for vegetarians.

Evaluation questions:
1. Differentiate between lacto-ovo vegetarians and vegans.
2. Explain three reasons why people adopt vegetarian diets.
3. List four Nigerian dishes that can be adapted for vegetarian diets.
4. What nutritional considerations should a caterer keep in mind when planning meals for strict vegetarians?
5. How would you respond to a client who requests a vegetarian menu but wants it to be filling and satisfying for meat-eaters at their event?

Summary:
Understanding different types of vegetarians and their nutritional needs is essential for caterers to create appropriate and satisfying menus for this growing dietary preference.

topics.title: Special Menu - Pregnant and Lactating Women lactating mothers; Guidelines for planning meals.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the nutritional needs of pregnant women, describe the nutritional requirements of lactating mothers, and apply guidelines for planning appropriate meals for these special groups.

Introduction:
Pregnancy and lactation are critical periods in a woman's life when nutritional needs increase significantly. As future caterers, understanding these needs will help you provide appropriate meals that support maternal and child health.

Content:
Pregnant women have increased nutritional needs to support fetal development and maintain maternal health. Key nutrients and their importance include: protein for tissue development of the fetus and placenta (sources include beans, nuts, lean meats, and fish); folic acid for preventing neural tube defects (found in leafy vegetables, beans, and fortified cereals); iron to prevent anemia and support increased blood volume (sources include red meat, poultry, fish, and fortified grains); calcium for fetal bone development (found in milk, cheese, yogurt, and leafy greens); and vitamin D for calcium absorption (obtained from sunlight exposure, fatty fish, and fortified foods). Lactating mothers require additional nutrients to support milk production: increased fluid intake (at least 3 liters daily including water, soups, and milk); protein for milk synthesis (sources include eggs, meat, beans, and nuts); calcium-rich foods (dairy products, leafy greens, and small fish with bones); and vitamin C for iron absorption and immune support (found in citrus fruits, tomatoes, and peppers). Guidelines for planning meals for pregnant and lactating women include: frequent small meals throughout the day to prevent nausea and ensure adequate nutrient intake; adequate fluid consumption to prevent dehydration; foods rich in iron consumed with vitamin C sources to enhance absorption; avoidance of raw or undercooked foods to prevent infections; and culturally appropriate foods that are well-tolerated and enjoyed. A sample meal plan for a pregnant Nigerian woman might include: breakfast - moi-moi with pap and banana, lunch - jollof rice with chicken and vegetables, dinner - yam porridge with fish and spinach, with snacks including groundnuts and fruits throughout the day.

Class activity:
Students will create a one-day meal plan for a pregnant woman in her second trimester, considering typical Nigerian food preferences and availability. The plan must include breakfast, lunch, dinner, and two snacks, with specific attention to nutrient density and cultural appropriateness.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain why folic acid is particularly important during pregnancy.
2. List three nutritional requirements that increase significantly during lactation.
3. How would you modify a typical Nigerian menu to make it more suitable for a pregnant woman?
4. Explain the importance of fluid intake for lactating mothers.
5. A pregnant client complains of morning sickness and has difficulty keeping food down. What meal planning adjustments would you suggest?

Summary:
Proper nutrition during pregnancy and lactation is crucial for maternal health and fetal development, requiring careful meal planning that addresses increased nutrient needs.

topics.title: Special Menu - Infants and Toddlers for planning meals for infants and toddlers.
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify characteristics affecting the nutritional needs of infants and toddlers, list guidelines for planning meals for these age groups, and demonstrate appropriate food preparation techniques for young children.

Introduction:
Infants and toddlers represent a unique population with specific nutritional requirements and feeding challenges. As caterers, understanding these needs is essential whether planning for a daycare center or creating family meal advice.

Content:
Infants (0-12 months) and toddlers (1-3 years) have distinct characteristics that affect their nutritional needs: rapid growth and development requiring adequate nutrients; immature digestive systems needing easily digestible foods; small stomach capacities requiring frequent meals; developing taste preferences forming during this period; and increasing mobility requiring energy-dense foods. Guidelines for planning meals for infants include: exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months; introduction of complementary foods at six months starting with single-ingredient purees; gradual introduction of new foods one at a time to monitor for allergies; avoiding honey until after 12 months to prevent botulism; and ensuring foods are soft, smooth, and easily swallowed. For toddlers, guidelines include: three main meals and two to three small snacks daily; foods cut into small, manageable pieces to prevent choking; variety of foods to establish healthy eating habits; limited intake of sugary and salty foods; and adequate calcium and iron sources for bone development and blood formation. Nigerian examples of appropriate foods include: for infants - smooth pap with breastmilk, pureed yam, mashed beans with palm oil; for toddlers - soft eko with beans, well-cooked rice with stew, mashed plantain with fish. Food preparation techniques include: steaming vegetables to preserve nutrients; mashing or pureeing foods for younger infants; removing bones and tough skins; avoiding excessive spices; and ensuring proper food safety to prevent contamination.

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to prepare age-appropriate meals for both an 8-month-old infant and a 2-year-old toddler using locally available ingredients. They will demonstrate proper food preparation techniques and explain their nutritional considerations.

Evaluation questions:
1. List three characteristics of infants that affect their nutritional needs.
2. Explain why complementary foods should be introduced at six months of age.
3. Describe appropriate food preparation techniques for infants.
4. How would you modify a typical Nigerian stew to make it suitable for a toddler?
5. What safety precautions should be taken when preparing meals for young children?

Summary:
Infants and toddlers have unique nutritional requirements that change rapidly during their first years of life, requiring specialized meal planning and preparation techniques.

topics.title: Special Menu - Adolescents
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to describe the characteristics of adolescents, list their nutritional requirements, and plan a day's menu that meets these needs while considering Nigerian food preferences.

Introduction:
Adolescence is a period of rapid growth and development with unique nutritional challenges. Understanding these needs is crucial for caterers working with schools, youth programs, or families with teenagers.

Content:
Adolescents, typically aged 10-19 years, have specific characteristics that affect their nutritional needs: rapid growth spurts requiring increased energy and nutrients; hormonal changes affecting appetite and food preferences; increased physical activity levels in some adolescents; developing body image concerns that may affect eating habits; and social influences that can shape food choices. Nutritional requirements for adolescents include: increased protein for muscle development (sources include meat, poultry, fish, eggs, and legumes); adequate calcium for bone development (found in milk, cheese, yogurt, and leafy greens); iron to support increased blood volume and prevent anemia (sources include red meat, poultry, fish, and fortified cereals); zinc for growth and immune function (found in meat, nuts, and whole grains); and adequate calories to support growth and activity levels. A day's menu for Nigerian adolescents might include: breakfast - akara with pap and bread, mid-morning snack - groundnuts and banana, lunch - jollof rice with chicken and vegetables, afternoon snack - fruit and yogurt, dinner - yam with vegetable soup and fish, evening snack - moi-moi. This menu provides adequate protein, complex carbohydrates, healthy fats, and essential micronutrients. When planning meals for adolescents, caterers should consider: adequate portion sizes to meet increased energy needs; inclusion of iron-rich foods consumed with vitamin C to enhance absorption; limited intake of sugary drinks and snacks to prevent excessive weight gain; culturally appropriate foods that will be accepted by the target population; and education about balanced nutrition to support healthy eating habits throughout life.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to plan a one-day menu for a boarding school with 200 adolescents aged 14-16. The menu must be nutritionally balanced, culturally appropriate, and cost-effective, with consideration for different food preferences and dietary restrictions.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain why adolescents have increased nutritional requirements compared to younger children.
2. List three key nutrients that are particularly important during adolescence and explain their functions.
3. How would you modify a traditional Nigerian menu to make it more appealing to adolescents while maintaining nutritional value?
4. What challenges might a caterer face when planning meals for adolescents, and how would you address them?
5. Create a balanced lunch menu for adolescents attending a secondary school in Nigeria.

Summary:
Adolescents have unique nutritional needs due to rapid growth and development, requiring careful meal planning that provides adequate nutrients while considering cultural preferences and food choices.

topics.title: Mid-Term Test / Open Day / Mid-Term Break
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to demonstrate their understanding of the topics covered so far through written and practical assessments, and showcase their learning to parents and visitors during the open day.

Introduction:
As we reach the midpoint of this term, it is time to assess our understanding of the concepts we've studied and celebrate our progress with an open day for parents and visitors.

Content:
The mid-term test will cover all topics studied so far: meal planning principles, special dietary needs including vegetarianism, nutrition for pregnant and lactating women, infant and toddler nutrition, and adolescent nutritional requirements. The test will include multiple-choice questions, short answer questions, and a practical component where students will demonstrate meal planning skills. For the open day, students will prepare and present dishes that demonstrate the concepts learned, including vegetarian options, meals suitable for pregnant women, and nutritionally balanced meals for different age groups. Students will explain their choices and nutritional considerations to visitors. The mid-term break provides an opportunity for rest and reflection on the first half of the term, as well as preparation for the topics to come after the break.

Class activity:
Students will participate in a cooking demonstration during the open day, preparing a three-course meal that showcases the different special dietary needs covered in class. Each student will be responsible for explaining one dish and its nutritional considerations to visitors.

Evaluation questions:
1. The mid-term test will assess students' knowledge of all topics covered so far.
2. During the open day, students will demonstrate practical skills in meal preparation and planning.
3. Students will explain the nutritional considerations behind their menu choices to visitors.
4. The break will allow students to rest and prepare for the second half of the term.
5. Students will reflect on their learning progress and identify areas for improvement.

Summary:
The mid-term test and open day provide opportunities for assessment and celebration of learning, while the break allows for rest and preparation for the remainder of the term.
